## Chapter 1

# CHAPTER XIX

CHAOS (1870)

One fine May afternoon in 1870 Adams drove again up St. James's Street wondering more than ever at the marvels of life. Nine years had passed since the historic entrance of May, 1861. Outwardly London was the same; outwardly Europe showed no great change. Palmerston and Russell were forgotten, but Disraeli and Gladstone were still alive, his friends were more prominent than ever, and reform ran riot. Never had the sun of progress shone so fair. Darwin was the greatest of prophets in the most evolutionary of worlds.

Yet at the Legation, Motley ruled; the long Adams reign was forgotten. Half the houses Adams had frequented from 1861 to 1865 were closed or closing. Death had ravaged one's circle. He found himself in a singular frame of mind—more eighteenth-century than ever—almost rococo—and unable to catch anywhere the cog-wheels of evolution. Experience ceased to educate. For English reforms he cared nothing; the reforms were themselves mediæval. He resented change. The tourist was the great conservative who hated novelty and adored dirt. He came back to London without a thought of revolution or restlessness or reform. He wanted amusement, quiet, and gaiety.

The first shock came lightly. Reeve refused the Gold Conspiracy: the article, he said, would bring half-a-dozen libel suits. The English press professed to be shocked in 1870 by the Erie scandal as it had professed in 1860 to be shocked by slavery, but when invited to support those abating the scandal, the English press said it was afraid. That a notorious story, taken bodily from an official document, should scare the *Edinburgh Review* into silence for fear of Jay Gould and Jim Fisk passed even Adams's experience of English eccentricity. The *Quarterly* also refused. He despatched the article at last to the *Westminster Review*.

He had been some weeks in London when he received a telegram from his brother-in-law at the Bagni di Lucca telling him that his sister had been thrown from a cab and injured, and that he had better come on. He started that night. Tetanus had already set in.

The last lesson—the sum and term of education—began then. He had never seen Nature, only her surface—the sugar-coating she shows to youth. Flung in his face with the harsh brutality of chance, the terror of the blow stayed by him thenceforth for life. He found his sister, a woman of forty, as gay and brilliant in the terrors of lockjaw as she had been in the careless fun of 1859. Hour by hour the muscles grew rigid, while the mind remained bright, until after ten days of fiendish torture she died in convulsion.

Society being immortal could put on immortality at will. Adams being mortal felt only the mortality. Nature enjoyed it, played with it; the horror added to her charm; she liked the torture, and smothered her victim with caresses. The hot Italian summer brooded outside, the hills and vineyards of the Apennines bursting with mid-summer blood. For many thousands of years, on these hills and plains, Nature had gone on sabring men and women with the same air of sensual pleasure.

Impressions like these are not reasoned in the mind; they are felt as part of violent emotion. The first serious consciousness of Nature's gesture—her attitude towards life—took form then as a phantasm, a nightmare, an insanity of force. For the first time, the stage-scenery of the senses collapsed; the human mind felt itself stripped naked, vibrating in a void of shapeless energies, with resistless mass, colliding, crushing, wasting, and destroying what these same energies had created and labored from eternity to perfect. The idea that any personal deity could find pleasure or profit in torturing a poor woman, by accident, with a fiendish cruelty known to man only in perverted and insane temperaments, could not be held for a moment. For pure blasphemy, it made pure atheism a comfort. God might be, as the Church said, a Substance, but He could not be a Person.

He travelled northwards with his friends and stopped at Ouchy to recover his balance. For the first time in his life, Mont Blanc for a moment looked to him what it was—a chaos of anarchic and purposeless forces—and he needed days of repose to see it clothe itself again with the illusions of his senses, the white purity of its snows, the splendor of its light, and the infinity of its heavenly peace. Before the illusions of Nature were wholly restored, the illusions of Europe suddenly vanished, leaving a new world to learn.

On July 4, all Europe had been in peace; on July 14, Europe was in full chaos of war. Mr. Gladstone was as much astounded as Adams. Only when he got up to Paris did he begin to feel the approach of catastrophe. Under one's eyes France cut herself adrift, and floated off, on an unknown stream, towards a less known ocean. The French regarded war as one of the fine arts; in Paris, in July, 1870, it was brought out like an opera of Meyerbeer. Every evening at the theatre the comedy was interrupted by order, and one stood up by order to join in singing the *Marseillaise* to order. Patriotism seemed to have been brought out of the Government stores, and distributed by grammes per capita.

He fled to England and took refuge in the profound peace of Wenlock Abbey, where Milnes Gaskell acted as Prior. The August sun was warm; the calm of the Abbey was ten times secular. Lying on the turf, the ground littered with newspapers, the monks studied the war correspondence. In one respect Adams had succeeded in educating himself: he had learned to follow a campaign.

There he received a letter from President Eliot inviting him to take an Assistant Professorship of History at Harvard. Adams knew nothing about history and much less about teaching, while he knew more than enough about Harvard College; and he wrote at once to thank President Eliot, with much regret that the honor should be above his powers. He sailed from Liverpool on September 1.

He found, on reaching home, that his article on the Session in the July *North American* had made a success, reprinted by the Democratic National Committee and circulated as a campaign document by the hundred thousand copies. He was henceforth in opposition, do what he might. His only reward consisted in being likened, in a Republican rebuttal, to a begonia—a plant remarkable for showy foliage and no useful purpose, conspicuous, insisting always on the most prominent positions. Adams would have greatly liked to be a begonia in Washington. When the *Westminster Review* for October brought him his Gold Conspiracy, also instantly pirated, here was a *tour de force*: two long, dry, quarterly articles for audiences in the hundred thousands; and not one person offering him so much as a congratulation, except to call him a begonia.

His whole family set on him to drag him away. His father interposed, his mother entreated, his brother Charles argued and urged that Henry had done at Washington all he could possibly do, that a few years in Cambridge would give him personal weight, that the chief function was not teaching but editing the *North American Review* coupled with the professorship. The good people who thought it did matter had a sort of right to guide; one could not reject their advice.

"But, Mr. President," urged Adams, "I know nothing about Mediæval History."

With courteous manner and bland smile Mr. Eliot mildly but firmly replied, "If you will point out to me any one who knows more, Mr. Adams, I will appoint him." The answer was neither logical nor convincing.

So, at twenty-four hours' notice, he broke his life in halves again to begin a new education, on lines he had not chosen, in subjects for which he cared less than nothing; in a place he did not love, and before a future which repelled. He had reached cross-roads of education which all led astray. Grant's administration wrecked men by thousands, but profited few. The period was poor in purpose and barren in results.

## Chapter 2

# CHAPTER XX

FAILURE (1871)

Far back in childhood, Henry Adams could recall his first visit to Harvard College, when his mother drove him out to visit his aunt, Mrs. Everett, in the old President's House on Harvard Square. The boy remembered a marble greyhound in the corner. The house had an air of colonial self-respect that impressed even a nine-year-old child.

When Adams closed his interview with President Eliot, he asked the Bursar about his aunt's old drawing-room, for the house had been turned to base uses. He took it. Above him, his brother Brooks had rooms.

For the next nine months the Assistant Professor had no time to waste on comforts or amusements. Between Gurney's classical courses and Torrey's modern ones lay a gap of a thousand years, which Adams was expected to fill. Down to the moment he took his chair and looked his scholars in the face, he had given, as far as he could remember, an hour, more or less, to the Middle Ages.

Not that his ignorance troubled him. He knew enough to be ignorant. A parent gives life, but as parent, gives no more. A murderer takes life, but his deed stops there. A teacher affects eternity; he can never tell where his influence stops. A teacher must either treat history as a catalogue, a record, a romance, or as an evolution; and whether he affirms or denies evolution, he falls into all the burning faggots of the pit. He makes of his scholars either priests or atheists, plutocrats or socialists, judges or anarchists, almost in spite of himself. In essence incoherent and immoral, history had either to be taught as such—or falsified.

Adams wanted to do neither. He had no theory of evolution to teach, and could not make the facts fit one. He knew that the man who should solve the riddle of the Middle Ages and bring them into the line of evolution from past to present would be a greater man than Lamarck or Linnæus; but history had nowhere broken down so pitiably. Since Gibbon, the spectacle was almost a scandal. For all serious purpose, it was less instructive than Walter Scott and Alexandre Dumas.

The lecture system to classes of hundreds, which was very much that of the twelfth century, suited Adams not at all. The number of students whose minds were of an order above the average was, in his experience, barely one in ten. He would try to cultivate this tenth mind, though necessarily at the expense of the other nine. He acted on the rule that a teacher who knew nothing of his subject should not pretend to teach what he did not know, but should join his students in trying to find the best way of learning it.

History is a tangled skein that one may take up at any point and break when one has unravelled enough; but complexity precedes evolution. The *Pteraspis* grins horribly from the closed entrance. He took as victims half-a-dozen highly intelligent young men and began with the beginning. The boys worked like rabbits, and dug holes all over the field of archaic society; no difficulty stopped them; unknown languages yielded before their attack. As pedagogy, nothing could be more triumphant; but their teacher knew that his wonderful method led nowhere. Their science had no system, since its subject was merely antiquarian. Try as hard as he might, the professor could not make it actual.

The Germans were crowning their new emperor at Versailles, and the Assistant Professor of History had nothing else as his stock in trade. He imposed Germany on his scholars with a heavy hand. The seven years he passed in teaching seemed to him lost.

As a professor, he regarded himself as a failure. He had succumbed to the weight of the system. He quitted the university at last, in 1877, with a feeling that, if it had not been for the invariable courtesy and kindness shown by every one in it, he should be sore at his failure. Yet nothing in the vanity of life struck him as more humiliating than that Harvard College, which he had persistently criticised, abused, abandoned, and neglected, should alone have offered him a dollar, an office, an encouragement, or a kindness. He could teach his students nothing; he was only educating himself at their cost.
